Nothing is required. Codacy will handle the migration automatically.

Copilot now spans five core tiers, and the headline monthly fees are unchanged from the pre-June structure – though GitHub has since layered on a sixth option above Pro+. In July 2026, cost-analysis firm CloudZero documented the arrival of a new Copilot Max tier priced at US$100 a month, aimed squarely at the heaviest individual users and agentic power-workflows that were blowing through Pro+’s allotment. What differs across the lineup is the size of the included premium-request allotment baked into each tier and the dollar value of AI Credits each plan receives. The table below summarises the published 2026 plan structure. [...] GitHub’s AI Credits act as a prepaid buffer, and the buffer has grown more generous than the headline fee suggests. Reporting from StartupHub.ai in May 2026 detailed how each paid tier now stacks a “base” credit allowance with a bonus “flex” allowance: Pro’s US$10 fee converts into US$10 of base credits plus US$5 of flex credits, for US$15 total; Pro+’s US$39 fee buys US$39 base plus US$31 flex, for US$70 total; and the newer Max tier’s US$100 fee buys US$100 base plus US$100 flex, for a full US$200 in spendable credits. Spend within the buffer and the experience feels unchanged. Spend beyond it and you either pay overage at the listed token rates (or US$0.04 per additional premium request, depending on how the consumption is classified) or hit a spending limit you have configured. There [...] GitHub was careful to frame the change as cost-neutral at the base. “Base plan pricing is not changing,” the company stated in its announcement, noting that Copilot Pro remained US$10 a month, Pro+ stayed at US$39, Business held at US$19 per user, and Enterprise stayed at US$39 per granted seat. Organizations rolling out agentic command line tools like Anthropic’s Claude Code and

# GitHub Copilot Impact Analysis: Prove ROI That Survives

*Written by: Mark Hull, Co-Founder and CEO, Exceeds AI | Last updated: September 11, 2026*

## How To Measure GitHub Copilot’s Impact

A defensible GitHub Copilot impact analysis follows a connected, seven-step sequence that moves from goals to financial outcomes.

1. Define the outcome before the tool. Decide what success looks like for your organization before touching the data.
2. Pick a comparison design. Choose a before/after or cohort design, and document why that design fits your environment.
3. Control for confounders. Account for project complexity, developer tenure, staffing changes, release seasonality, and concurrent tool changes.
4. Measure at four levels. Track adoption, developer productivity, engineering outcomes, and business value as distinct signal layers.
5. Watch for commit inflation. Flag rising commit and line counts that do not reflect durable engineering value.
6. Track AI-touched code over 30+ days. Capture the maintenance and incident story that point-in-time quality metrics miss.
7. Account for the full AI toolchain. Include Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, Windsurf, and other tools that sit alongside Copilot.

## What The Credible Evidence Actually Says

[The Peng et al. (2023) randomized controlled trial (arXiv:2302.06590) recruited developers to implement an HTTP server in JavaScript and found the Copilot group finished 55.8% faster](https://github.com/AvneeshSarwate/ai-econ-research/blob/main/summaries/peng-2023-github-copilot-productivity.md). The internal validity is strong for that bounded, greenfield task. The external validity is weak because the study measured one well-specified task and excluded quality, maintenance, debugging, architecture, and integration work. It is best read as a task-specific upper bound rather than an organization-wide productivity multiplier.

[Cui et al. (2024, SSRN 4945566) ran three randomized field experiments across Microsoft, Accenture, and a Fortune 100 electronics firm with 4,867 developers and found approximately 26% more pull requests completed](https://anylearn.cc/lessons/coding-agents-productivity-evidence). This is the most rigorous enterprise evidence available for autocomplete-era Copilot. The adoption-cohort figures of 78% and 151% merged-PR jumps are associations, not causal proof, because developers who adopt AI tools early may already be more productive.
